0.title: Labels and the Soul
0.essay:
Depression, anxiety, OCD, ADHD: these labels are now part of everyday speech. Many Christians carry one, or love someone who does, and wonder what the Bible has to say to it. This study starts from the label and asks four questions of each: what is meant by it, how it is usually treated, what the Bible says, and what the biblical way forward is.

Why start from the label?

A diagnosis is often where a person’s story with the struggle begins in earnest. It can bring relief (“so this has a name”), or fear, or a sense of being defined by it. The Bible does not use modern psychiatric terms, but it speaks with great depth about the experiences behind them: sorrow, fear, compulsion, trauma, craving, confusion. It sees us as embodied souls, body and heart together, living in a world where both bodies and minds are broken. And it shows us a Saviour who “will not break” a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3).

Getting help

Throughout this study the same pattern is followed. Seek out a biblical counsellor, through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation (for example ACBC or CCEF in the US, Biblical Counselling UK in Britain), and tell your pastor. A good biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up, so that any bodily cause is found and treated, and will then help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. If the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is not a failure of faith. If you are having thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself, or are losing touch with reality, get medical or emergency help today, then involve your pastor and a counsellor.

The study Biblical Counseling covers many of the same struggles from the counsellor’s side; this one is written for the person with the label and those who love them.

The chapters

Before the Labels: How to Think About a Diagnosis; Depression; Anxiety Disorders and Panic Attacks; Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD); Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD); Bipolar Disorder; Eating Disorders: Anorexia and Bulimia; Addiction; Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD); Borderline Personality Disorder; Schizophrenia and Psychosis; Self-Harm and Suicidal Thoughts; and Autism.

For reflection

Which of these labels touches your life, or the life of someone you love? What do you most hope the Bible will say to it?

1.title: Before the Labels: How to Think About a Diagnosis
1.essay:
Before we look at any single label, we need a way of thinking about labels themselves. A diagnosis can be a real kindness or a heavy weight, depending on how we understand it and how we hold it.

What a diagnosis is, and is not

When a doctor says “depression” or “obsessive-compulsive disorder”, they are naming a pattern. Over many years doctors noticed that certain experiences tend to come together: low mood with broken sleep, lost appetite and a sense of worthlessness; or unwanted thoughts that return again and again, with rituals that try to quiet them. Naming the pattern helps doctors compare treatments, and for many sufferers it brings real relief: I am not the only one.

But a diagnosis is not a verdict on a person’s worth, and it is not a full explanation of them. It describes what is happening, not who someone is before God.

How the labels are made

Most psychological diagnoses are defined in two reference books: the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (the DSM, now in its fifth edition) and the World Health Organization’s International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11). Each condition is described by a checklist: which symptoms, how many, for how long, and how much they disrupt life. For most of these conditions there is no blood test or brain scan that settles the matter.

The manuals are careful and useful. But a description is not an explanation. To say someone has “generalised anxiety disorder” tells us what they experience: persistent worry that is hard to control. It does not tell us why. The cause may lie in the body, circumstances, past hurts, habits of thought, or what the heart loves and fears, and most often in several together. The boundaries are drawn by panels of experts and revised from edition to edition. A label is a map of the ground, not the ground itself.

Body and soul together

Scripture teaches that we are embodied souls. “The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature” (Genesis 2:7). Paul can say, “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16): two sides of one person, each affecting the other.

So a sick body can darken the mind (a thyroid problem, a hormonal change, lack of sleep), and a troubled heart can weigh on the body. David, hiding his sin, wrote, “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). Both directions are real. Neither cancels the other.

Suffering and sin distinguished

We live in a groaning creation, where even believers “groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:20–23). Bodies and minds break. Much of what a diagnosis names is suffering: things that happen in us or to us that we did not choose. To treat suffering as if it were sin is cruel, as Job’s friends learned when God rebuked them.

Yet the heart is never merely passive. In every trouble we respond, trusting God or turning elsewhere, fearing him or fearing other things. Some patterns do involve sin, and Christ forgives sin freely. So the wise question is rarely “Is this illness or is it sin?” as though only one could be true. It is: what here is suffering, to be met with comfort; what here is the heart’s response, to be brought to Christ; and what here is the body, to be cared for?

Scripture sufficient, medicine ordinary

“All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16–17). God’s Word gives us all we need to know God, understand ourselves and live faithfully in any trouble: that is its sufficiency.

Scripture does not claim to be a medical textbook. Jesus took doctors for granted: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:12). Luke was “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), and Paul told Timothy to take a little wine “for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments” (1 Timothy 5:23). Medical care is one of God’s good gifts to a fallen world. Receiving it is not a failure of faith.

Why the counsellor comes first

This study follows one order throughout. First, seek a biblical counsellor through your church, or through a biblical counselling organisation, and tell your pastor. The deepest questions a diagnosis raises are questions of the soul: is God still for me, what do I do with this fear? Second, a good biblical counsellor will ask for a medical check-up, so that any bodily cause is found and treated: not handing the person over, but caring for the whole person. If the doctor recommends treatment, including medication, receiving it is no failure of faith. Third, the struggle itself is worked through from God’s Word, with the counsellor as God’s instrument.

There is one exception. Thoughts or plans of suicide, self-harm, losing touch with reality, severe weight loss in an eating disorder, or a high, reckless state that puts someone in danger: get medical or emergency help today, and then involve your pastor and counsellor.

Holding a label humbly

A label is a tool, not an identity. It is better to say “I struggle with depression” than “I am depressed” as though that were the deepest thing about you. A Christian’s deepest name is “in Christ”. Labels can also become prisons or excuses. And humility runs both ways: doctors can be wrong, and so can counsellors. God alone sees the whole: “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14).

A man in his forties was diagnosed with depression after his business failed. At first the word was a comfort; then it became a wall that ended every conversation. A wise counsellor did not take the label away. He helped him see it as one true description among several: a body worn out by stress, a real grief, and a heart that had quietly made success its refuge. Each was met in its own way, and the man found Christ more solid than the business had ever been.

For reflection

Has a diagnosis, yours or someone else’s, been more of a help or more of a weight? Why? How does knowing that we are embodied souls change the way you think about mental struggles? What is the difference between saying “I have this” and “I am this”?

2.title: Depression
2.essay:
Depression is one of the most common labels in any doctor’s surgery, and one of the most common hidden burdens in any church. Scripture does not use the word, but it knows the darkness well, and it knows a Saviour who does not break bruised reeds.

What the label means

A doctor diagnosing depression (in the manuals, “major depressive disorder”) is looking for a low mood, or a loss of interest and pleasure in almost everything, that lasts most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks. Other signs come with it: disturbed sleep and appetite, exhaustion, poor concentration, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, and often thoughts of death. It is very common: the World Health Organization estimates that around one adult in twenty is depressed at any one time, and many more will be at some point in life.

Postnatal depression is depression in the year after having a baby. It affects roughly one mother in ten, and some fathers too. It is different from the “baby blues”, the tearfulness of the first fortnight that soon passes. A rare and serious condition, postpartum psychosis, involves confusion or losing touch with reality and is a medical emergency.

The label describes a pattern; it says nothing about the sufferer’s worth.

How it is usually treated

For mild depression doctors often begin with self-help, exercise and talking therapies. The best known is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which looks at patterns of thinking and behaviour. For moderate or severe depression, antidepressant medication is commonly offered, most often an SSRI, usually with a talking therapy. These take several weeks to work and help many, though not all. Severe cases may need hospital care. Treatment helps a great many people, though relapse is common.

What the Bible says

Scripture is full of believers in the dark. The psalmist cries, “I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears” (Psalm 6:6). Psalm 88 ends without any resolution at all: “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). Such prayers tell the sufferer that this darkness can be brought to God just as it is.

Elijah, after his great victory on Carmel, ran for his life, sat under a broom tree and “asked that he might die” (1 Kings 19:4). God’s first answer was not a rebuke. An angel touched him and said, “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). Sleep and food first, a gentle question and a renewed task later.

The Bible also helps us distinguish. Much depression is suffering: grief, illness, exhaustion, being sinned against, or a body that is not working as it should in a fallen world (Romans 8:22). Some is bound up with sin: guilt hidden rather than confessed, as in Psalm 32, or bitterness nursed, or a life built on something that has collapsed. Often it is both, and in every case the heart matters. Depression preaches its own message (God has forgotten me, I am worthless), and Scripture answers it without denying the pain.

This commentary’s view: some Christians treat all depression as a spiritual failing, while others hand it entirely to medicine. This commentary holds that much depression is suffering, not sin; that the body matters and medication has its place; and that the deepest needs of the depressed person are still met in Christ through his Word.

An example

A young mother found that, weeks after her second child was born, she could not stop crying, could not sleep even when the baby slept, and felt she was failing everyone. Ashamed, she told no one until an older woman in her church noticed and gently asked. Her pastor put her in touch with a biblical counsellor, who urged her to see her doctor that week. The doctor diagnosed postnatal depression and she accepted treatment. Meanwhile the counsellor read Psalm 42 with her and helped her name the lies she was believing, and the church organised meals and nights of sleep. Recovery took months, not days, but she later said she had never known Christ’s gentleness so clearly.

The biblical way forward

The first word is Christ. Of him it is written, “a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3). He knows sorrow from the inside: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). The Son of God has entered this darkness, borne our sin and risen, so it cannot have the last word.

Then Scripture gives practices. Lament: pour out your heart honestly to God, as the Psalms do. Truth to the mind: talk back to your soul, as the psalmist does: “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him” (Psalm 42:5). Rest and the body: sleep, food, daylight and movement, as with Elijah. Small steps of obedience and community: let others carry you. Repentance where sin is part of the story, knowing that confession brings relief (Psalm 32:5). And the means of grace: the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and gathered worship, even when feelings are flat. Hope may come slowly. It is still hope.

Getting help

Seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK in Britain, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask you to see your doctor, to look for bodily causes. If the doctor recommends treatment, including antidepressants, receiving it is not a failure of faith. Work through the struggle itself from God’s Word with your counsellor, for it is sufficient for what you face. If you have thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself, or if a new mother is confused or out of touch with reality, get medical or emergency help today, then involve your pastor. For more, see the studies Depression and Biblical Counseling.

For reflection

Which message does depression preach most loudly, and what does Scripture say in reply? Why might God have fed Elijah before he spoke to him? Who in your church might be carrying this quietly, and how could you come alongside them?

3.title: Anxiety Disorders and Panic Attacks
3.essay:
Everyone knows worry. An anxiety disorder is worry or fear that has grown so large and so constant that it rules a person’s days. The Bible speaks often to fear, and it does so with great tenderness.

What the label means

“Anxiety disorders” is a family name. Taken together they are the most common mental health conditions. Three are especially familiar.

Generalised anxiety disorder is excessive worry about many things (health, money, family, work) that is hard to control and present on most days for at least six months. It often brings restlessness, tiredness, tense muscles and broken sleep.

Panic disorder involves repeated panic attacks: sudden surges of intense fear that peak within minutes, with a pounding heart, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, trembling and a sense of dying or losing control. The disorder includes the ongoing dread of the next attack, which often leads people to avoid places where one might happen.

Social anxiety disorder is intense, lasting fear of being watched, judged or embarrassed in ordinary social situations, strong enough to make people avoid them.

Each label describes a pattern of experience, not a measure of someone’s faith.

How it is usually treated

The main talking therapy is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). For panic and social anxiety it usually includes gradual exposure: facing feared situations step by step, so the person learns the danger is smaller than it feels. Medication is common, most often an SSRI or a related antidepressant, taken for months. Sedatives called benzodiazepines are used only briefly because of the risk of dependence. Doctors also look for physical contributors such as an overactive thyroid or too much caffeine. Many people improve a great deal, though anxiety often flares again at times of stress.

What the Bible says

Scripture is honest about fear. David, alone among the Philistines, “was much afraid of Achish the king of Gath” (1 Samuel 21:12), and he later wrote, “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3). Notice: when I am afraid. Fear came, and David brought it to God. Another psalm describes something close to panic: “My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me” (Psalm 55:4–5). In Gethsemane our Lord himself was “in agony” and “his sweat became like great drops of blood” (Luke 22:44). Strong feelings of distress are not in themselves sin.

We are embodied souls, and the body’s alarm can misfire in a fallen world (Romans 8:22). That calls for patience, not shame.

Yet Scripture also looks beneath the surface. Jesus asks, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” (Matthew 6:27). It can be fed by what the heart has made its safety: money, health, or other people’s approval. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). So the Bible both comforts the fearful and gently asks what the heart is fearing, loving and trusting. Its command not to be anxious comes with an invitation: “in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6).

An example

A man in his thirties had his first panic attack in a supermarket queue. He was sure he was dying. Tests at hospital found nothing wrong with his heart, and the attacks kept coming. Soon he avoided shops, then church. His pastor connected him with a biblical counsellor, who asked him to see his GP; the doctor explained panic disorder and offered treatment. The counsellor helped him see that the attacks were frightening but not dangerous, and that his heart was clutching at control. Together they read Mark 4, where Jesus sleeps in the storm and then stills it. Step by step, with a friend beside him, he went back to the shops and to church, and the attacks became rarer. When one came, he learned to pray Psalm 56:3 and let it pass.

The biblical way forward

Christ is the answer to fear before any technique. He says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you… Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27). He has dealt with the deepest fear of all, the fear of judgment, by bearing it for us, so “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

From there, Scripture shapes practice. Cast your cares on him specifically and often: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Live one day at a time, for “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” (Matthew 6:34). Fill the mind with truth: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you” (Isaiah 26:3). Face fears in small steps of obedience, trusting God in each one; this fits well with what good exposure therapy teaches. Do not hide: “Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad” (Proverbs 12:25). And where fear of man or love of control has crept in, confess it and receive mercy. The aim is not a fearless life but one where fear drives us to God.

Getting help

Seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if it has none, through an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK in Britain, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask you to see your doctor, because thyroid, heart and other physical causes need ruling out. If the doctor recommends therapy or medication, receiving it is no failure of faith. Work through the fear itself from God’s Word with your counsellor, for it is sufficient for what you face. If anxiety comes with thoughts of ending your life, or chest pain you are not sure about, get medical or emergency help today. See also the study Contentment and Anxiety.

For reflection

What does Psalm 56:3 teach about the difference between feeling afraid and sinning? What, if anything, is your heart relying on to keep you safe instead of God? How could you help someone in your church take one small, brave step?

4.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
4.essay:
People often joke about being “a bit OCD” about tidiness. The real condition is no joke. It is a tormenting cycle of unwanted thoughts and the rituals used to quiet them, and in Christians it often attacks the very things they hold most dear.

What the label means

Obsessive-compulsive disorder has two parts. Obsessions are unwanted thoughts, images or urges that intrude again and again and cause great distress: fear of contamination, fear of harming someone, fear that something terrible will happen, unwanted sexual or violent images, or a need for things to feel exactly right. Compulsions are actions or mental acts done to reduce the distress or prevent the feared outcome: washing, checking, counting, repeating, arranging, seeking reassurance, or mentally reviewing and “undoing” a thought. The relief is real but brief, and the cycle tightens. For a diagnosis it must take up much time (often over an hour a day) or seriously disrupt life. OCD affects around one or two people in a hundred, and usually begins in the teens or early adulthood.

Two forms matter especially for Christians. Intrusive thoughts are the unwanted thoughts themselves, often about the very things the person finds most horrifying. Religious scrupulosity is OCD that fixes on sin and salvation: fear of having committed the unforgivable sin, compulsive confessing, repeated prayers that never feel “right”, endless checking of one’s motives, and an inability to rest in forgiveness.

The label describes a pattern, not the person’s true desires: the thoughts torment precisely because they are the opposite of what the person wants.

How it is usually treated

The leading therapy is exposure and response prevention (ERP), a form of CBT. The person gradually faces the thing that triggers the obsession and resists the compulsion, learning that the anxiety rises and then falls on its own, and that the feared outcome does not follow. It is demanding but well supported. Medication is also common: SSRIs, often at higher doses than for depression, and sometimes an older drug, clomipramine. Many improve markedly, though OCD often needs ongoing management.

What the Bible says

Scripture distinguishes temptation from an unwanted intrusion. James explains how sin grows: “each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin” (James 1:14–15). Sin begins with the heart’s willing movement towards what it wants. An intrusive thought that the person hates and fights is not that. The thought is not the sin.

Scrupulosity needs the gospel applied precisely. Jesus did speak of an unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32), but that is a settled, hardened rejection of Christ, not the frightened fear of a believer that they might have done it. The very fear is evidence that they have not. And Scripture speaks directly to the accusing conscience: “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20).

Church history offers a well-known example. Martin Luther as a young monk confessed for hours at a time, searching out every possible sin, and found no peace, until he came to see that righteousness is a gift received in Christ, not an achievement checked and rechecked. John Bunyan described similar torment with blasphemous thoughts. Whatever their exact diagnosis, both found rest not in certainty about themselves but in Christ.

An example

A student began to fear that a passing blasphemous thought meant she had committed the unforgivable sin. She prayed the same prayer of repentance dozens of times a day, and asked friends again and again whether she was saved. Her pastor recognised the pattern and connected her with a biblical counsellor, who asked her to see her doctor; she was referred for assessment and began ERP. The counsellor did not keep answering the same question. Instead she said, kindly and firmly, “You are in Christ. That is settled. We will not reopen it today.” Together they studied the gospel, not the fear. Slowly she learned to let the thought come and go, and to rest in Christ’s promise rather than in the feeling of certainty.

The biblical way forward

The heart of the answer is that Christ’s work is finished and does not need to be checked. “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). Our standing rests on his perfect obedience and sacrifice, not on how clean our thoughts feel or how sincere our last prayer was.

So the practices of faith take a particular shape here. Confess once, then believe the promise: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). Repeating confession to get the right feeling is a compulsion, not repentance. Name the thought and let it pass, without arguing, analysing or neutralising it; taking “every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5) does not mean wrestling every intrusion, but refusing to let it set the agenda. Turn from reassurance-seeking to the once-for-all promise; this is also what ERP teaches. Accept uncertainty: faith rests on his word, not a feeling. Stand in freedom: “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1). Progress is often slow, with setbacks, but Christ is patient with his struggling children.

Getting help

Seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if it has none, through an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK in Britain, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask you to see your doctor; a referral for ERP or medication may well follow, and receiving it is not a failure of faith. Alongside any medical care, the counsellor will help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. If the distress brings thoughts of suicide or self-harm, get medical or emergency help today. See also the study Biblical Counseling, which has a chapter on OCD and intrusive thoughts.

For reflection

Why is an unwanted intrusive thought different from temptation as James describes it? How does Christ’s finished work answer the urge to keep checking and confessing? If a friend kept asking you for reassurance, how could you love them without feeding the cycle?

5.title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
5.essay:
Some people go through something terrible and find, months or years later, that it has not stayed in the past. It comes back uninvited, in dreams, in sudden panic, in a body that will not stand down. The one who bears the scars of the cross is near to them.

What the label means

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a pattern that can follow a frightening, life-threatening or violating event: war, a serious accident, assault, sexual abuse, a violent death witnessed, a disaster. Doctors describe four groups of symptoms. The event is relived, in flashbacks, nightmares and intrusive memories. The person avoids people, places and thoughts that bring it back. Thinking and mood change: guilt, shame, numbness, a sense that the world is entirely dangerous. And the body stays on high alert, with poor sleep, irritability, a sharp startle and constant watchfulness. The diagnosis is made when these last for more than a month and seriously disrupt life.

Most people who go through a trauma recover without developing PTSD, but studies in Western countries suggest around one adult in twenty to one in fifteen will have it at some point. Like every label in this study, it describes a pattern of experience and behaviour. It is not a verdict on a person’s worth, nor a weakness of character, nor a full explanation of who they are.

How it is usually treated

The treatments with the strongest research behind them are trauma-focused talking therapies: trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, and EMDR (eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing). These help the person face the memory safely and loosen the false conclusions it has left. Certain antidepressants (SSRIs) are also used, and some medicines help with nightmares. Many people improve a great deal, though not all, and recovery is often gradual.

What the Bible says

The Bible does not use the word trauma, but it is full of traumatised people and is honest about what terror does. David prays, “My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me” (Psalm 55:4–5). Paul writes of a time in Asia when “we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself” (2 Corinthians 1:8). After she was violated, Tamar “lived, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom’s house” (2 Samuel 13:20).

Scripture explains why trauma lodges so deeply. We are embodied souls: “the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). What happens to the body reaches the heart, and what the heart has seen shows in the body.

So the Bible distinguishes carefully. What was done to a person is the sin of the one who did it, not of the victim. Flashbacks and nightmares are suffering, not sin. Yet the heart’s responses still matter: what has the person come to believe about God and about themselves? Joseph is a striking example. Sold by his brothers and forgotten in prison, he did not pretend it had not happened. He named his son Manasseh, “For,” he said, “God has made me forget all my hardship” (Genesis 41:51), and years later, weeping, he could say, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The memory remained; its power to rule him did not.

An example

A woman in her forties was hit by a car at a crossing. Her injuries healed, but she could no longer drive, woke shouting most nights, and snapped at her children. Her pastor listened and urged her to see her doctor, who referred her for trauma-focused therapy. Her church found a biblical counsellor who met with her weekly. She learned to pray the psalms of terror as her own, and slowly named the lie beneath her fear, that God had looked away that day, and set against it his promise to be with her in the waters and the fire. A year later the nightmares were rare. She drove again.

The biblical way forward

The first thing to know is who Christ is to the wounded. He was himself betrayed, stripped, beaten and killed. He knows violence from the inside. “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). When he rose, he kept his scars and showed them: “Put your finger here, and see my hands” (John 20:27). Of him it is said, “a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench” (Isaiah 42:3).

From there, Scripture gives a path. Lament: put the horror into words before God, as the psalmists did. He has “kept count of my tossings” and put “my tears in your bottle” (Psalm 56:8). Truth to the mind: name the false conclusions (I am dirty, I am to blame, nowhere is safe) and answer them with God’s word, slowly. Safety and rest: sleep, routine and safe people are not unspiritual; “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8). Community: a church that believes and protects them. Forgiveness belongs in the story, but in God’s time, and never as a demand to pretend or to stay near danger. And hope: one day “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4).

Getting help

Seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask you to see your doctor so that sleep, physical symptoms and any related depression are checked; if the doctor recommends trauma therapy or medication, receiving it is not a failure of faith. The struggle itself is worked through from God’s sufficient Word. If you are thinking of ending your life or harming yourself, or abuse is still happening, get help today: emergency services or a crisis line first, then your pastor. The study Biblical Counseling has a fuller chapter on trauma and sexual abuse.

For reflection

What has a frightening experience led you to believe about God or about yourself, and what does Scripture say in reply?

How does it help to know that the risen Christ still bears his wounds?

How could your church be a safer place for those who carry trauma?

6.title: Bipolar Disorder
6.essay:
Bipolar disorder can take a person to the heights and to the depths, sometimes within a single year. Scripture does not name it, but it speaks of a God who does not change, and of a Saviour who keeps hold of his people when their own minds will not hold steady.

What the label means

Bipolar disorder (once called manic depression) is a condition of episodes: periods of depression and periods of mania or hypomania, with stretches of relatively normal mood between. Mania is more than a good mood. It brings an elevated or irritable state lasting days or weeks, with much less need for sleep, racing thoughts, rapid speech, grand ideas, and reckless decisions about money, sex or driving. In severe mania a person may lose touch with reality. Hypomania is a milder form. Bipolar I involves at least one full manic episode; bipolar II involves hypomania and major depression.

Around one or two people in a hundred have bipolar disorder. It usually begins in the late teens or twenties, runs strongly in families, and tends to recur across life. The risk of suicide is significantly raised, especially in the depressed phases. The label describes a pattern; it does not tell you who the person is, and it is no verdict on their worth.

How it is usually treated

Treatment is usually long term. Mood stabilisers, especially lithium, and certain antipsychotic medicines are the mainstay, along with others such as lamotrigine for preventing depression; antidepressants are used with caution because they can trigger mania. Psychological help (learning warning signs, family support, regular routines, protecting sleep) makes a real difference. Most people do far better with treatment, though relapses happen, and stopping medication suddenly often brings a new episode.

What the Bible says

Scripture tells us we are embodied souls, and that the fall reaches all the way into the body: “the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves” (Romans 8:22–23). A brain whose mood regulation has broken is part of that groaning. Bipolar disorder is not a sign of weak faith or a punishment, and its swings are not simply moral choices.

Some have read the condition of King Saul, troubled by “a harmful spirit” (1 Samuel 16:14), as bipolar disorder. That is unwise. Saul’s trouble is described as God’s judgment on a king who had rejected his word, and we have no right to treat a suffering believer as Saul. Nor should we assume demons are at work when a doctor finds an illness.

A closer window is Elijah. Fresh from the victory on Carmel, he ran for his life, sat under a broom tree, “And he asked that he might die” (1 Kings 19:4). God’s first response was not rebuke but sleep and food: “Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7).

Yet the heart is still in view. Mania can feel wonderful, and the heart may love it, resent the medicine that ends it, or excuse the harm done in it. Depression can whisper that God has gone. Scripture calls the person, as far as they are able, to humility about their own mind, to wise self-government (“he who rules his spirit” is better “than he who takes a city”, Proverbs 16:32), and to repentance for real wrongs, while giving great grace for what the illness itself does.

An example

A young man in his twenties began to sleep only three hours a night, spent his savings on a business idea in a week, and told his church he had a special message from God. Then he crashed into a depression so deep he stopped eating. His family took him to the doctor, and he was diagnosed with bipolar I and started on lithium. He stopped taking it once, with painful results. A biblical counsellor and his pastor walked with him for two years. They helped him see that medicine was humble stewardship, not unbelief, that he should apologise to those he had hurt while manic, and that his worth did not rise or fall with his moods. He keeps a sleep routine and a written plan his wife and elders know about.

The biblical way forward

For someone whose inner world can swing so far, the first comfort is the steadiness of God. “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). With the Father of lights “there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). The person’s grip on God may loosen in an episode, but Christ’s grip on them does not; his mercies “are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:23).

Practices grow from that. Rest and rhythm: regular sleep is one of the strongest protections, and God “gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Humble self-knowledge: let trusted people help you watch for warning signs. Truth to the mind: in depression, preach hope to yourself (Psalm 42:5); in rising mania, test grand ideas and supposed revelations by Scripture and wise counsel before acting. Repentance where there is sin, and quick, generous forgiveness among those who were hurt. The means of grace: Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship carry a person through seasons they cannot carry themselves.

This commentary’s view: some Christians fear that long-term medication for the mind shows a lack of trust in God. This commentary holds that bipolar disorder involves a real bodily illness, that receiving the treatment a doctor recommends, including long-term mood stabilisers, is good stewardship of the body God gave, and that this works together with, not against, the ministry of the Word to the heart.

Getting help

Seek a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will insist on medical care; for bipolar disorder a psychiatrist’s ongoing treatment is normally essential, and taking it is not a failure of faith. Alongside any medical care, the counsellor will help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. Do not stop medication without your doctor. Mania with danger, psychosis, or any thoughts of suicide need medical or emergency help today, then pastor and counsellor. The study Biblical Counseling has a chapter on severe mental illness.

For reflection

How does the unchanging faithfulness of God comfort someone whose moods change so much?

Where is the line between what the illness does and what the heart chooses, and why does that line need both grace and honesty?

How could a church help a member keep a plan for staying well?

7.title: Eating Disorders: Anorexia and Bulimia
7.essay:
Eating disorders turn food, one of God’s kindest gifts, into a battlefield. They are among the most dangerous conditions in this study, and they touch the deepest questions of the heart: who am I, what am I worth, and who is in control? The Bible answers each of those questions with Christ.

What the label means

Anorexia nervosa is marked by restricting food to the point of a significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight, and a distorted view of one’s own body; a person may be dangerously thin and still see themselves as too large. Bulimia nervosa involves repeated episodes of binge eating, with a sense of loss of control, followed by attempts to undo them: vomiting, laxatives, fasting or extreme exercise. Weight is often normal, so it can stay hidden. Binge eating disorder involves regular binges without the purging, usually with deep shame; it is the most common of the three.

These conditions most often begin in the teens or early twenties and are more common in girls and women, though men and boys suffer too. Anorexia has one of the highest death rates of any mental disorder, through starvation’s effects on the heart and through suicide. Bulimia can disturb the body’s salts and damage the heart, gut and teeth. The labels describe patterns; they do not define the person, and they are no measure of anyone’s worth or faith.

How it is usually treated

Treatment begins with the body: medical monitoring and, in anorexia, careful restoration of weight, sometimes in hospital when life is at risk. For young people with anorexia, family-based treatment, in which parents take charge of meals for a season, has good evidence. For adults, specialised cognitive behavioural therapy is widely used. Bulimia and binge eating usually respond best to eating-disorder-focused CBT; some medicines (for example, certain antidepressants) are used alongside. Many people recover fully, but recovery is often long, with setbacks along the way.

What the Bible says

Scripture begins with goodness. God made our bodies and called his work “very good” (Genesis 1:31). Food is his gift: “everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:13–14).

The Bible also exposes the heart beneath the behaviour, gently. Eating disorders are often attempts to find control, safety, purity or relief: a way to feel clean, acceptable or numb. Scripture would call these good longings looking for satisfaction in a broken cistern (Jeremiah 2:13). It also warns that harsh treatment of the body looks like wisdom but is “of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23). And it overturns the verdict of appearance: “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

So both suffering and sin are in view, carefully distinguished. A starving brain cannot think clearly, and much of what the person experiences is the illness itself. Yet the heart’s trust matters: in whom, or in what, am I looking for worth and peace? Hannah, provoked year after year, “wept and would not eat” (1 Samuel 1:7). Her grief went into her appetite. Her help came when she poured out her soul before the LORD. And when Jesus raised Jairus’s daughter, his first instruction was tender and practical: he “told them to give her something to eat” (Mark 5:43).

An example

A seventeen-year-old girl, a keen runner and top student, began cutting out foods after a comment about her shape. Within a year she was dangerously underweight but felt she was finally in control. Her parents noticed her fainting and took her to the doctor, who referred her to a specialist team; for a time her parents had to plate every meal and sit with her. A biblical counsellor met with her and her parents together. Slowly she put words to her fear that, without control, she would be nothing, and learned that in Christ she was already loved, accepted and complete. She slipped back more than once. Two years on she eats with her family, runs for joy rather than penance, and leads a small group for younger girls at church.

The biblical way forward

Christ meets the person with an eating disorder as the true Bread. “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). He offers what the disorder promised and could not give: real control (his, loving and wise), real cleanness (by his blood), and a worth that does not depend on a number. “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). That is a liberating word: this body belongs to a Lord who cares for it, so it may be fed, rested and treated kindly.

Practices follow. Receive food as obedience and gift: eating the meal plan is a step of faith, “received with thanksgiving.” Truth to the mind: write down the disorder’s lies and set God’s word against each. Confession and light: secrecy feeds the disorder; telling trusted people starves it, and where there is sin there is mercy for the one who confesses (Proverbs 28:13). Community: eating together, without comments on bodies. Change is usually slow, and setbacks are not the end.

Getting help

Seek a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will insist on a medical check-up straight away, because eating disorders do serious harm to the body; if the doctor recommends specialist treatment, hospital care or medication, receiving it is not a failure of faith. Alongside any medical care, the counsellor will help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. Severe anorexia, fainting, chest pain, or any thought of suicide or self-harm needs medical or emergency help today. The studies Eating Disorders and Biblical Counseling go further.

For reflection

What does the disorder promise, and how does Christ give the real thing?

Why does it matter that God called the body “very good”?

How might your family or church speak about food and bodies in a way that heals rather than harms?

8.title: Addiction
8.essay:
Addiction is one of the oldest human stories: something that promised freedom becomes a master. Scripture saw it long before modern medicine named it, and its answer is not a technique but a Person: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

What the label means

Doctors speak of a substance use disorder when a person keeps using alcohol or drugs despite clear harm: they lose control over how much they use, crave it, give up other things for it, and keep going though it damages health, work and relationships. Tolerance (needing more) and withdrawal (feeling ill without it) often develop. The same pattern can form around behaviours. Gambling disorder is formally recognised; compulsive sexual behaviour, including heavy pornography use, is recognised by the World Health Organization, though experts still debate how best to name it.

Addiction is common: alcohol problems alone affect a substantial minority of adults in many countries. Repeated use changes the brain’s reward and self-control systems, which is why stopping is so hard. The label describes a pattern; it does not sum up a person, and it is not a verdict on their worth.

How it is usually treated

Withdrawal from alcohol or certain sedatives can be dangerous, even life-threatening, so stopping heavy use should be done with medical help. Medicines can help: methadone or buprenorphine for opioid addiction, and naltrexone or acamprosate to reduce relapse in alcohol dependence. Talking therapies (such as cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing), mutual-help groups such as twelve-step fellowships, and residential programmes are widely used. Relapse is common, and recovery often takes several attempts; many people do achieve lasting freedom.

What the Bible says

Scripture describes addiction with startling accuracy. Proverbs paints the drunkard who has been beaten and does not feel it, and wakes only to say, “When shall I awake? I must have another drink” (Proverbs 23:35). Peter names the principle: “whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19). Paul refuses that slavery: “I will not be dominated by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12).

The Bible holds together what our culture tends to pull apart. Addiction is truly bondage: the body and brain have been shaped by repeated use, and the person cannot simply decide to stop. It is also, at its root, worship: the heart has gone to a broken cistern for comfort, escape or pleasure that only God can give (Jeremiah 2:13), and Scripture does not hesitate to call drunkenness and sexual immorality sin. Many addictions began in suffering, which needs care too.

This commentary’s view: some Christians call addiction a disease and avoid the word sin; others call it sin and dismiss the language of illness. This commentary holds that addiction is both a real sin for which a person is responsible and a real slavery that has taken hold of body and mind. That is why the answer must be both forgiveness and deliverance, both repentance and patient help, including medical help.

The prodigal son is the great picture. He spent everything on what consumed him, ended among the pigs, then “came to himself” (Luke 15:17) and turned home. He did not have to clean himself up first: “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him” (Luke 15:20).

An example

A man in his fifties, a deacon, had hidden his drinking for years. After a fall at home, his wife found the bottles and called the pastor. His doctor arranged a supervised withdrawal and prescribed medication to reduce cravings. His pastor connected him with a biblical counsellor and two older men in the church who met him weekly. He confessed to his wife and the elders, stepped down from office for a season, and saw what the drink had been doing for him: numbing the grief of his son’s death that he had never brought to God. He relapsed once, at a funeral, and phoned one of the men that same night. Three years on he is sober.

The biblical way forward

The gospel speaks first. “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Christ died for drunkards, gamblers and the sexually enslaved, and rose to break the power of sin as well as its guilt. “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14). Freedom rests on his work, not on the addict’s willpower.

Then come practices. Repentance and confession: bring it into the light, to God and to others; “confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Radical steps: remove access, install accountability, change routes and habits, as Jesus taught about cutting off what causes us to stumble. A new fullness: “do not get drunk with wine… but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18); the heart needs a greater pleasure, not just an empty space. Community: daily encouragement, “that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). Hope in the fight: God “will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13). A relapse is a reason to run back to the Father, not to give up.

Getting help

Seek a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask you to see your doctor, and with alcohol or sedatives you must not stop heavy use suddenly without medical advice. If the doctor recommends detox, medication or a programme, receiving it is not a failure of faith. Alongside any medical care, the counsellor will help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. An overdose, dangerous withdrawal, or thoughts of suicide need emergency help today. The study Biblical Counseling has chapters on alcohol and drugs, gambling, and pornography.

For reflection

What has your heart turned to for comfort or escape instead of God?

Why does the Bible call addiction both sin and slavery, and why do we need both words?

Who could you ask to walk with you, and to whom could you be that friend?

9.title: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
9.essay:
Some people’s minds seem to run at a different speed from the world around them: easily pulled away, restless, quick to act before they think. ADHD is the name now given to that pattern. Scripture speaks to it with a patient Saviour who is not exasperated with his scattered disciples, and with a church where the weaker members are cared for.

What the label means

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is described as a neurodevelopmental condition: a difference in how the brain develops that shows from childhood. Doctors look for two groups of features. Inattention: trouble keeping focus on tasks that are not interesting, careless mistakes, losing things, forgetting appointments, starting much and finishing little. Hyperactivity and impulsivity: fidgeting, restlessness, talking over others, interrupting, acting or spending on the spur of the moment. To be diagnosed, the pattern must begin in childhood, show up in more than one setting, and clearly get in the way of life.

Around one child in twenty is diagnosed in many countries, more often boys, and in many cases the difficulties continue into adult life, though hyperactivity often settles into inner restlessness. ADHD runs strongly in families. There is honest debate about whether it is now over-diagnosed in some places and missed in others, especially in girls. The label describes a pattern of attention and behaviour. It is not a verdict on a person’s intelligence, character or worth, nor a full explanation of them.

How it is usually treated

For young children, guidance and training for parents comes first: clear routines, calm consistent discipline and practical help at school. For older children and adults, medication is widely used. Stimulant medicines (methylphenidate and amphetamine-based medicines) reduce symptoms for most people while they are taken; non-stimulant medicines are an alternative. They do not cure ADHD and have side effects, such as poor appetite and sleep, which need watching. Adults are often helped by cognitive behavioural therapy, coaching, and practical systems: lists, reminders, breaking tasks into small steps.

What the Bible says

The Bible does not mention ADHD, but it gives us the categories to understand it. We are embodied souls, made from the dust and given the breath of life (Genesis 2:7). Our bodies, brains included, share in a creation that is “groaning together” (Romans 8:22). Some of what is labelled ADHD may be part of that God-given variety; some reflects the weakness of a fallen world. Either way, a child who cannot sit still is not thereby a rebel, and an adult who forgets is not thereby lazy.

At the same time, Scripture never treats a difficulty as removing the heart from view. A distractible person can still love God and neighbour, and can still sin in the ways their weakness makes easy: impatience, careless words, broken promises shrugged off, anger at those who ask too much. The Bible calls everyone to wisdom: “Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time” (Ephesians 5:15–16).

We should not diagnose people in the Bible, but the apostle Peter shows how Jesus deals with an impulsive follower. Peter stepped out of the boat and sank, spoke when he should have listened, and cut off a servant’s ear. Jesus rebuked him at times, but he did not give up on him. “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32). The same Peter became a rock in the church. And Paul’s instruction to the church fits ADHD well, because it asks us to tell different needs apart: “admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14).

An example

A man in his thirties had always been told he was clever but lazy. He lost jobs for missed deadlines, and his wife felt she was running the house alone. A biblical counsellor at a neighbouring church listened, asked him to see his doctor, and he was diagnosed with ADHD and tried medication, which helped. The counsellor helped him see two things together: that his struggle was real and not simply laziness, and that he still needed to repent of the excuses and the irritability with which he had protected himself. He learned to ask forgiveness quickly and to thank God for the energy and quick-wittedness that are also part of how he is made.

The biblical way forward

The first word is Christ. He is gentle with people who struggle to keep up: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). His acceptance does not depend on finishing the list. Someone told all their life to try harder needs to hear that in Christ they are already received and loved. That is not an excuse; it is the safe ground on which to grow.

From there come practical steps. Wise structure: routines, reminders, short tasks and fewer commitments are not unspiritual crutches but wise use of time. Truth to the mind: answer the old voices (“useless”, “hopeless”) with what God says. Repentance where there is sin: for unkind words, excuses and broken promises, with the confidence that he forgives. Small obedience: faithfulness in one thing today. Community: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Families and churches can help with reminders and patience, and let restless people serve with their energy. The means of grace: short, regular times in the Word and prayer suit a busy mind better than heroic plans that collapse.

This commentary’s view: some Christians are uneasy about medicating children’s behaviour, and others see ADHD medicine as simply treating a bodily weakness. This commentary holds that a careful diagnosis and medication a doctor recommends may be received with thanks and is no failure of faith, while parents and churches should also attend to sleep, screens, structure and the shaping of the heart, which no tablet can do.

Getting help

Seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask for a medical assessment, since sleep problems, anxiety, depression and other conditions can look like ADHD. If the doctor recommends treatment, including medication, receiving it is not a failure of faith. The struggles of the heart are worked through from God’s sufficient Word. If there are thoughts of suicide or self-harm, get medical help today, then speak to your pastor.

For reflection

Where might you have called someone lazy or rebellious when they were weak, or excused your own sin as weakness?

How does Jesus’ patience with Peter encourage you?

What practical structure, or what practical help from others, could make faithfulness easier this week?

10.title: Borderline Personality Disorder
10.essay:
Few labels sound as harsh as “personality disorder”, and few people suffer as intensely as those who carry this one. Behind it is usually a person terrified of being left, whose emotions run like a flood. Christ is the one who will never leave, and his church can learn to love such people well.

What the label means

Borderline personality disorder (BPD; in some countries called emotionally unstable personality disorder) describes a long-standing pattern of instability in three areas: emotions, relationships and sense of self. Typical features are an intense fear of being abandoned; close relationships that swing between idealising someone and feeling utterly let down by them; an unsteady sense of who one is; harmful impulsive actions; repeated self-harm or suicidal behaviour; rapid, intense mood changes; a chronic feeling of emptiness; sudden strong anger; and, under stress, feelings of unreality or suspicion.

Perhaps one or two people in a hundred meet the criteria, and many more are seen in mental health services. It usually becomes clear in the late teens or early adulthood. Painful early experiences, such as abuse, neglect or chaotic homes, are common in the background, together with an emotionally sensitive temperament, though neither is true of everyone. The outlook is better than the name suggests: long-term studies show that most people improve a great deal over the years. The label describes a pattern; it is not a verdict that a person is broken beyond repair or of less worth.

How it is usually treated

The main treatment is structured psychological therapy over a long period. Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) teaches skills for bearing distress, managing emotions, staying in the present and handling relationships, and has good evidence for reducing self-harm. Mentalisation-based therapy and schema therapy are also used. No medicine treats BPD itself, but doctors may prescribe for depression, anxiety or other conditions alongside it.

What the Bible says

Scripture sees this person whole. They are made in God’s image and are embodied souls; their temperament and their history have truly shaped them. Many have been sinned against deeply, often as children, and that was the sin of others, not theirs. The flood of feeling is in large part suffering, and Scripture is not shocked by strong emotion (see Psalm 22).

Yet the Bible also speaks to the heart’s responses, because they matter for the person and for those around them. Fear of abandonment can turn into clinging, testing and controlling; hurt can turn into rage. Scripture says, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26), and pictures a life without restraint as painful: “A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls” (Proverbs 25:28). Self-control is not a personality type but fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23), which means it can grow in anyone who belongs to Christ.

The deepest question beneath BPD is often, “Who am I, and will anyone stay?” Jesus met a woman at a well whose relationships had broken again and again. He told her the truth plainly: “You have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband” (John 4:18). Yet he neither despised her nor walked away. He offered her living water, and she ran to tell others, “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did” (John 4:29).

An example

A woman in her twenties, abused as a girl, had a long record of intense friendships that ended in fury, and of cutting herself after each one. A small group at church loved her, then felt worn out by late-night crisis messages. Her pastor arranged for her to see her doctor, who referred her for DBT, and a biblical counsellor began meeting her every week. The church agreed a plan together: steady, predictable care from several people, not rescue by one. Slowly she learned to name her feelings to God in the psalms instead of acting on them, to ask forgiveness for outbursts, and to believe that God’s love did not rise and fall with her moods. She still has hard days, but her friendships now last.

The biblical way forward

Christ answers the fear of abandonment at its root. “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). His love is not earned and cannot be lost by a bad day. Nothing, Paul says, “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). Union with Christ gives a fixed point: you are his, whatever you feel.

From that ground the steps follow. Lament: bring the flood of feeling to God in words, as the psalmists did, rather than turning it on yourself or others. Truth to the mind: catch the all-or-nothing thoughts (“they hate me”, “I am nothing”) and test them against what is true. Repentance where there is sin: for rage, manipulation or harm done, received with grace and not as condemnation. Small steps of obedience: one honest conversation, one urge not acted on. Community: a church that loves steadily, with several carers and clear, kind limits, which protect both the person and those who help. The means of grace, which keep telling the same good news when feelings change hourly.

Getting help

Seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will ask for a medical check-up and will want you under your doctor’s care; if the doctor recommends a therapy such as DBT, or medication for depression or anxiety, receiving it is not a failure of faith. The heart struggle itself is worked through from God’s sufficient Word. Self-harm and suicidal thoughts are common with this condition: if you are in danger, get emergency help today, then speak to your pastor and counsellor.

For reflection

How does Christ’s promise never to leave answer the fear of being abandoned?

Why does a church need both steady love and clear limits to care for someone with this struggle?

Where do strong feelings in your own life need to be brought to God in words rather than acted out?

11.title: Schizophrenia and Psychosis
11.essay:
Psychosis is perhaps the most frightening of all the labels in this study, both for the one who suffers it and for those who love them. It can seem to take the person away. But no illness can take a believer out of Christ’s hand, and the church is called to stay close.

What the label means

Psychosis means losing touch with reality. Its main features are hallucinations (most often hearing voices others cannot hear), delusions (fixed false beliefs, for example that one is being watched, persecuted or controlled), and confused thinking and speech. Psychosis is a symptom, not one illness: it can come with severe depression, bipolar disorder, drug use (cannabis and stimulants especially), dementia and some physical illnesses.

Schizophrenia is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms persist for six months or more, usually alongside what doctors call negative symptoms (loss of motivation, flattened emotion, withdrawal from others) and difficulties with memory and concentration. It affects a little under one person in a hundred during their life, usually beginning between the late teens and early thirties. It is not a “split personality”, and people with schizophrenia are far more often victims of violence than causes of it. The course varies: some recover well, many have episodes that come and go, and some live with lasting disability. The label describes a pattern of experience. It never tells you a person’s worth, and it is not the whole of who they are.

How it is usually treated

Antipsychotic medication is the foundation of treatment and helps most people, especially with voices and delusions; clozapine is used when other medicines fail. Side effects such as weight gain, drowsiness and stiffness are real and need careful management. Early intervention teams, cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis, family work and practical support all improve the outlook. A first episode needs urgent assessment.

What the Bible says

The Bible does not describe schizophrenia in modern terms, but it gives the framework. We are embodied souls, “the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7), and the mind works through a body that shares in a groaning creation (Romans 8:22–23). When the brain is sick, perception and thought can break. That is suffering, not personal sin. A person hearing voices is not guilty for hearing them.

Scripture also shows that not every disturbance has the same cause. Matthew records that people brought to Jesus “all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them” (Matthew 4:24). The Gospels distinguish illness from demonic oppression; they do not treat them as the same. The man among the tombs in the region of the Gerasenes was under demonic power, and Christ’s authority over it is plain: afterwards he was “sitting there, clothed and in his right mind” (Mark 5:15). That is not a picture of modern psychosis, but it shows the Lord’s compassion for a tormented outcast and his power to restore a mind.

The heart is still there, even in severe illness. Even in episodes, a person can trust, pray, fear and love, and God deals with them as his child. The Psalms give voice to the isolation: “You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). God put that cry in his book.

This commentary’s view: some Christians assume that voices and strange beliefs are always demonic and should be met with deliverance prayer rather than medicine. This commentary holds that Scripture distinguishes sickness from demonic oppression, that psychosis should be presumed to need urgent medical care, and that prayer belongs alongside that care, never in place of it.

An example

A university student, a keen Christian, began to believe that messages in hymns were warnings meant only for him and stopped sleeping. His parents brought him home and, with their pastor’s support, took him to the emergency department. He was diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis, later schizophrenia, and began medication. A biblical counsellor met with him when he was well enough, helping him hold on to simple truths, keep a routine, and talk about his fear that God had abandoned him. Members visited him in hospital. He has had two further episodes, but he knows he belongs to Christ and to his church.

The biblical way forward

Begin with Christ. He touched lepers and went to the man no one else would approach. He holds his people when they cannot hold their own thoughts together: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13). When a person cannot find words to pray, “the Spirit helps us in our weakness” (Romans 8:26). Their salvation does not depend on a clear mind but on a faithful Saviour.

Then Scripture gives a path. Medical care taken faithfully, as stewardship of the body. Simple truth: short verses and familiar hymns often reach a troubled mind when long arguments cannot; “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Rest and rhythm: sleep, regular meals and avoiding cannabis and other drugs. Community: visits, practical help, a seat kept at church, and support for exhausted families. Jesus told his hearers to invite “the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind” (Luke 14:13); the church should be a place where the mentally ill are welcomed, not avoided. Repentance where there is sin, handled gently, for what was truly chosen. Hope: one day every mind in Christ will be whole.

Getting help

Psychosis is an emergency: if someone is losing touch with reality, or is a danger to themselves or others, get medical or emergency help today, then contact your pastor. For ongoing care, seek a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will work alongside the psychiatrist, not against them; receiving antipsychotic medication is not a failure of faith, and it should never be stopped without the doctor. The heart’s struggles, such as fear, shame and doubt, are worked through from God’s sufficient Word. The study Biblical Counseling has a chapter on severe mental illness.

For reflection

Why does it matter that the Gospels distinguish sickness from demonic oppression?

How does God’s faithfulness comfort someone whose mind is not clear?

What would it take for your church to welcome and stay with a member living with schizophrenia?

12.title: Self-Harm and Suicidal Thoughts
12.essay:
Some people hurt their own bodies to cope with pain inside. Some wish they were dead, or plan to die. If that is you, you are not beyond help, and the Lord who was wounded for us does not turn away from you.

If you are in danger now: if you have a plan to end your life, have harmed yourself seriously, or cannot keep yourself safe, get help today. Call the emergency services (999 in the UK, 112 across Europe, 911 in North America) or go to an emergency department. You can call a crisis line at any hour: in the UK and Ireland, Samaritans on 116 123; in the US, 988. Tell someone you trust and do not stay alone. Then, once you are safe, speak to your pastor.

What the label means

Strictly, self-harm and suicidal thoughts are not diagnoses but experiences, which come with many conditions, especially depression, and also with crises, losses and shame. Self-harm means deliberately hurting oneself: cutting, burning, hitting, or taking an overdose. It is most common in teenagers and young adults. People describe it as a way to cope with overwhelming feelings, to feel something when numb, to gain a sense of control, or to punish themselves. Not everyone who self-harms wants to die, but self-harm greatly raises the risk of later suicide and must always be taken seriously.

Suicidal thoughts range from a passive wish not to wake up, to active thoughts of ending one’s life, to a definite plan. Most people who have them do not act on them, but the move from thought to action can be quick, especially with alcohol, drugs or easy access to means. Asking someone directly whether they are thinking of suicide does not put the idea in their head; it often brings relief. These words describe what someone is going through. They do not measure their worth or their faith.

How it is usually treated

Care begins with safety: assessing risk, making a written safety plan (warning signs, ways to cope, people to call), and removing or locking away means such as stockpiled tablets. Underlying conditions such as depression are treated. Talking therapies help: cognitive behavioural therapy for suicidal thinking, and dialectical behaviour therapy, which has good evidence for reducing self-harm. Wounds need proper medical care.

What the Bible says

Scripture is honest that believers can wish to die. Job cursed the day of his birth. Elijah sat under a broom tree, “And he asked that he might die” (1 Kings 19:4). Jonah said, “it is better for me to die than to live” (Jonah 4:3). Paul wrote that “we despaired of life itself” (2 Corinthians 1:8). God did not cast any of them off. To Elijah he sent sleep, food and his own presence.

The Bible also tells us our lives and bodies are not our own to destroy. “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Suicide is a grave sin, the taking of a life that belongs to God; yet the right first response to someone in crisis is not a lecture but care, presence and hope. Some have taught that suicide cannot be forgiven, but Scripture nowhere says so; still, no one should treat that as permission.

Self-harm appears in Scripture too, and always as a sign of bondage. The prophets of Baal “cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them” (1 Kings 18:28). The tormented man among the tombs was “always crying out and cutting himself with stones” (Mark 5:5). Often beneath self-harm is a sense that pain must be paid for, or that one deserves to suffer. The gospel answers that at the root: the punishment has been paid by another. “he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).

One scene says it all. When an earthquake opened the prison in Philippi, the jailer drew his sword to kill himself. Paul cried out, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here” (Acts 16:28). That night the jailer heard the gospel and was baptised. God’s word to the despairing is not condemnation but rescue.

An example

A sixteen-year-old girl had been cutting her arms in secret for a year, and one night told a youth leader she did not want to be alive. The leader stayed with her, called her parents and, together, they went to the emergency department that night. She was assessed, made a safety plan, and was treated for depression. A biblical counsellor met her each week. Under the cutting lay shame, and a belief that she had to hurt to make up for failing. Slowly, through Isaiah 53 and the cross, she began to believe that Christ had borne what she thought she deserved. She still has scars and hard nights, but now she texts her mum instead of reaching for a blade.

The biblical way forward

Christ is the heart of it. He was “a man of sorrows” (Isaiah 53:3), who said in the garden, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). He knows the darkness. His wounds speak a better word than ours: they say the debt is paid, and that you are loved enough for him to die for you. “A bruised reed he will not break” (Isaiah 42:3).

Then the steps. Safety first: keep the plan, tell people, remove the means. Lament: pour out the pain to God in words, as Psalm 88 does, instead of on your body. Truth to the mind: answer the lies (“everyone would be better off without me”, “I deserve this”) with God’s word. Repentance and grace: where there is sin, Christ forgives it fully; self-punishment adds nothing to his cross. Community: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2); families and churches should not leave a struggling person alone. The means of grace: the Lord’s Supper proclaims his body broken for us, so that we need not break our own.

Getting help

Emergency help comes first: if there is a plan, serious harm, or you cannot stay safe, call the emergency services or a crisis line today (999, 112 or 911; Samaritans 116 123; 988 in the US), then speak to your pastor. After that, seek a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will ask for a medical check-up and ongoing medical care; receiving treatment, including medication, is not a failure of faith. The heart’s struggle is worked through from God’s sufficient Word. The study Biblical Counseling has a fuller chapter on suicide and self-harm.

For reflection

What does God’s care for Elijah under the broom tree tell you about how he treats the despairing?

How does the cross answer the belief that pain must be paid for by the one who suffers it?

Who would you call, today, if you or someone you love were not safe?

13.title: Autism
13.essay:
Autism is different from the other labels in this study. It is not a passing illness or a disorder of the heart, and it is certainly not a sin to be counselled away.
