It is a lifelong difference in how a person is made, which brings real gifts and real struggles. Scripture speaks of a God who forms each person and a church in which every member is needed.

What the label means

Autism (the formal diagnosis is autism spectrum disorder) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference that shapes how a person experiences the world and relates to others. Doctors look for two main areas. First, differences in social communication: finding it hard to read faces, tone of voice and unspoken rules, preferring plain and literal speech, and finding conversation and friendship tiring or confusing. Second, restricted and repetitive patterns: a strong need for routine and sameness, deep and focused interests, repeated movements, and often marked sensory differences, so that noise, light, touch or certain foods can be overwhelming, or barely noticed.

It is called a spectrum because it varies so widely. Some autistic people have little or no speech and need help with daily life all their lives; others have average or high ability, work, marry and raise families, and may not be diagnosed until adulthood. Estimates vary, but at least one person in a hundred is autistic, and recent counts in some countries are higher. It is diagnosed more often in boys, while girls are often missed. Autism is strongly genetic; it is not caused by vaccines or by poor parenting. Anxiety, depression, ADHD and sleep problems often come with it. The label describes how a person is wired. It is no measure of their worth, nor of their faith.

How it is usually treated

Because autism is part of who a person is, the aim is not cure but support. For children this may include speech and language therapy, occupational therapy for sensory and practical needs, structured early learning programmes (some of which are debated among autistic adults and professionals), and help at school. Adults may be helped by adjustments at work and practical support. There is no medicine for autism itself, but doctors may treat the anxiety, depression, sleep difficulties or ADHD that often come alongside it. Being understood is often the greatest help.

What the Bible says

The Bible says first that God is the maker of each person, mind included. “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:13–14). When Moses protested, “I am slow of speech and of tongue” (Exodus 4:10), God answered, “Who has made man’s mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11). God does not wait for us to be typical before he uses us.

Christians may ask how much of autism is simply the variety of God’s making and how much reflects the weakness of a fallen world. The honest answer is probably some of both, as it is for every one of us. Focus, honesty, faithfulness to routine and love of detail can be gifts. The sensory pain, the exhaustion of social life and the loneliness are part of the groaning of creation (Romans 8:22). What we must not do is treat the autism itself as sin. A meltdown under sensory overload is not a tantrum of defiance, and missing a social cue is not rudeness of heart.

Autistic people are, like everyone, both sinners in need of grace and, in Christ, saints loved by God. Their hearts face the same calls as everyone’s, to trust God and love others, but those calls come to them as they are made.

Scripture also shows the welcome the church owes. King David sought out Mephibosheth, “lame in both his feet”, and gave him a place: “he ate always at the king’s table” (2 Samuel 9:13). In the body of Christ, “the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable” (1 Corinthians 12:22).

An example

A woman diagnosed as autistic at forty had always found church exhausting: the crowded coffee time, the small talk, the unspoken expectations. She had been told she was cold and should try harder, and she often went home and cried. After her diagnosis, her pastor met with her to ask what would help. The church gave her a quieter place to sit, sent the order of service in advance, and stopped expecting her to mingle. Someone asked her to help keep the church accounts, which she did superbly. A biblical counsellor helped her with the anxiety and old hurts she carried, and with how to forgive those who had misunderstood her. She says that for the first time she feels she belongs.

The biblical way forward

The way forward begins not with fixing the person but with Christ’s welcome. “Welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God” (Romans 15:7). Jesus received children, the disabled and the outsider. In him an autistic believer is fully accepted, adopted and loved, and their place in his church is not on probation.

From there: Rest in God’s design: thank God for how he has made you, gifts and limits together. A welcoming church: clear and literal speech, predictable plans, quiet spaces, patience with differences, and roles that use real gifts. “God settles the solitary in a home” (Psalm 68:6), and the church is one of the homes he uses. Help with the struggles: anxiety and loneliness are common and can be addressed from Scripture, with lament, truth for the fearful mind, and steady friendship. “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you” (Psalm 55:22). Support for families: parents of autistic children are often tired and isolated, and need practical help and prayer. The means of grace, offered in ways the person can receive them.

Getting help

Autism itself is not something to be counselled away, but the struggles that often come with it, such as anxiety, loneliness, depression or hurt, can be. For these, seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if your church has none, through a biblical counselling organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the US or Biblical Counselling UK, and tell your pastor. A good counsellor will understand autism, and may ask for a medical check-up or a formal assessment; if the doctor recommends support or treatment for anxiety, depression or sleep, including medication, receiving it is not a failure of faith. Autistic people face a raised risk of suicide: if there are thoughts of ending life or of self-harm, get medical or emergency help today, then speak to your pastor.

For reflection

How does Psalm 139 shape the way you see an autistic person, or yourself?

What unspoken expectations in your church might make it hard for autistic people to belong?

Where could the gifts of an autistic member be welcomed and used?
